Amendment to the SSKIN Bundle Care Plan/template should be made based on findings of reassessments and clinical judgment. 5.8 Recognising Risk Made Easy Prompt screening/ risk assessment and timely implementation of pressure ulcer prevention and treatment strategies can reduce the risk and severity of pressure ulcers. People at risk include those who have one or a combination of conditions which compromise the body’s protective mechanisms against pressure loading. This includes the following; Protective Loss of Mechanisms Impaired mobility physical ability away from pressure. Impaired Sensation = ability to feel the need to move away from pressure = to move Impaired Circulation = conditions which impair the quality and quantity of blood feeding the skin and tissues Examples of Conditions • recent surgery, fracture/cast, prosthesis, CVA Including Parkinson’s, profound multiple disabilities, Spinal injury, falls/ collapse • Neurological or sensory deficits; CVA, MS, diabetes, spinal injuries, , motor neurone disease • Depression leading to lack of motivation to mobilise • Dementia/cognitively impaired • Hyperalgesia or neuropathic pain • Previous History of Pressure ulcers • Chronic anaemia / renal disease/ heart and lung disease • Peripheral vascular /arterial disease • Diabetes- Macro and micro circulation • Acute deterioration – dehydration, chest/ UTI/ wound infection, flu, winter vomiting disease hypovolemic shock, Impaired nutrition and/or dehydration • • End of Life- Skin Changes Life’s End (SCALE) 5.9 Risk Assessment and Clinical Judgement Waterlow Risk Assessment Tool This tool was developed by Judy Waterlow in 1988 to include a more comprehensive assessment of patient’s vulnerability to developing pressure ulcers. The tool like all other risk calculators has its limitations and is no substitute for sound clinical judgment. Systemic Infection - Patients with very severe sepsis or trauma or shock can develop widespread vasomotor paralysis causing peripheral shut down and multi-organ failure and sometimes death. Bacteria has been shown to become localised at the site of compression because capillary permeability is increased after pressure is released and thus local infection can embarrass the circulation and precipitate ischemia (MacGill, 2020) Non-concordance - Concordance is not a patient behaviour, but rather the interaction between the clinician and patient. Non-concordance occurs if a therapeutic partnership is not established and, therefore, denotes a failure of the interactions of the clinician. It is the responsibility of all healthcare professionals to advise patients of their risk status and care required to minimise risks so that patients feel empowered to play an active role in the prevention and management of pressure ulcers. A patient’s decision to decline certain aspects of their care plan does not negate their right to services. Good practice will be to work collaboratively towards a care plan that is accepted as appropriate by the multi- disciplinary team and the patient. Where there is a difference of opinion between the patient and/or carer and the team involved in their care this should be discussed and explored to see if there is any way to find an agreement between the differing views. It is important for staff to record the patient’s thoughts and feelings about the advice given as well as their understanding of the consequences of declining care as well as their reasons for declining care interventions. It may be the patient cannot sleep on an alternating mattress or is afraid to go to bed because they cannot easily get out of the bed during the night. paragraphs.context: Page 13 of 15 27/02/2026 Guidelines for Pressure Ulcer Risk Assessment - Adapted Waterlow Score Beta-blockers such as Propranolol or Metoprolol can cause vasoconstriction, which can compromise peripheral circulation. Cytotoxics these drugs will alter the normal cellular response to trauma or the ability to supply oxygen to the tissue. Nicorandil often used to treat angina, and has been associated with painful peri-anal, vulval and non-healing ulcers. When the treatment is stopped the ulcer usually goes on to heal. Epidurals will result in the total loss of sensation to the lower limbs and therefore put the patient at risk of pressure damage. Many of these patients need assistance with moving safely as their perception of where their limbs are is diminished. Score 4 SURGERY/TRAUMA There is the risk of pressure damage on the effected limb due to pain and loss of movement and the potential for fiction damage on the unaffected limb increases as a result of friction caused by over use (blisters formed trying push up the bed etc). Within the Community post-operative risks is not such a common risk factor. However, a common reoccurring trend has been identified when patients are visiting hospitals for out– patient treatments and are often sitting for hours at a time and so are at increased risk during these periods. These patients require close monitoring particularly if they are already at risk. Also, patients recently discharged from Acute hospitals are at increased risk in the first couple of days following discharge and it is important to review these patients as soon as possible to ensure adequate provision of equipment and care on discharge. Score 5 In this sub-score the risk may well only be temporary ‘high’, therefore, interventions to prevent any damage in this stage will aid recovery in the long run, as rehabilitation will not be slowed down by the presence of the ulcers. 6.
